claim: DunedinPACE demonstrated a high in-sample correlation with Pace of Aging to age 45 (r = 0.78).
source: DunedinPACE demonstrated a high in-sample correlation with Pace of Aging to age 45 (r = 0.78, Figure 1a).
evidence: The correlation coefficient is reported directly from the analysis of the Dunedin Study data.

claim: DunedinPACE shows improved fit to the 20-year Pace of Aging compared to the original DunedinPoAm version's fit to the 12-year Pace of Aging (in-sample correlation r = 0.6).
source: The value indicates improved fit of the DunedinPACE model to the 20-year Pace of Aging as compared to the original DunedinPoAm version's fit to the 12-year Pace of Aging (in-sample correlation r = 0.6).
evidence: Comparison of correlation coefficients between DunedinPACE and DunedinPoAm from the Dunedin Study data.

claim: DunedinPACE showed excellent test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.96 [0.93–0.98]) in replicate adult-blood-sample Illumina 450k datasets.
source: For DunedinPACE, reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.96 [0.93–0.98]; Figure 2).
evidence: ICC was calculated from 36 replicate samples in the GSE55763 dataset.

claim: The original DunedinPoAm showed good test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.89 95% CI [0.79–0.94]).
source: For the original DunedinPoAm, reliability was good (ICC = 0.89 95% CI [0.79–0.94]).
evidence: ICC was calculated from 36 replicate samples in the GSE55763 dataset.

claim: DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.97 [0.94–0.98] in the EPIC-EPIC database.
source: DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.97 [0.94–0.98] in the EPIC-EPIC database and 0.87 [0.82–0.90] in the 450k-EPIC database.
evidence: ICC was calculated from n=28 replicate EPIC-array datasets reported by Sugden et al., 2020.

claim: DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.87 [0.82–0.90] in the 450k-EPIC database.
source: DunedinPACE ICCs were 0.97 [0.94–0.98] in the EPIC-EPIC database and 0.87 [0.82–0.90] in the 450k-EPIC database.
evidence: ICC was calculated from n=350 replicates where one dataset was from Illumina 450k and the other from EPIC array.

claim: Chronologically older Understanding Society participants had faster DunedinPACE as compared to younger ones (r = 0.32).
source: Chronologically older Understanding Society participants had faster DunedinPACE as compared to younger ones (r = 0.32, Figure 3A).
evidence: Correlation was calculated from Understanding Society Study data (n=1175, age range 28-95).

claim: The correlation between chronological age and DunedinPACE was threefold larger as compared to the correlation for the original DunedinPoAm (r = 0.11).
source: This correlation was threefold larger as compared to the correlation for the original DunedinPoAm (r = 0.11).
evidence: Comparison of correlation coefficients from Understanding Society Study data.

claim: Among NAS participants with repeated-measures DNA methylation data (n = 536), DunedinPACE increased by b = 0.021 (SE = 0.003) per 5 years of follow-up.
source: Among NAS participants with repeated-measures DNA methylation data (n = 536), DunedinPACE increased by b = 0.021 (SE = 0.003) per 5 years of follow-up, or approximately 0.2 standard deviation units, similar to what we previously reported for the original DunedinPoAm (Belsky et al., 2020).
evidence: Within-individual change was analyzed using repeated-measures DNA methylation data from the NAS cohort.

claim: DunedinPACE was weakly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Horvath clock (r = 0.13).
source: DunedinPACE was weakly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Horvath clock (r = 0.13) and somewhat more strongly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Hannum and Levine clocks (Hannum r = 0.26; PhenoAge r = 0.36).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data (n=1175).

claim: DunedinPACE was somewhat more strongly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Hannum clock (r = 0.26).
source: DunedinPACE was weakly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Horvath clock (r = 0.13) and somewhat more strongly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Hannum and Levine clocks (Hannum r = 0.26; PhenoAge r = 0.36).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data (n=1175).

claim: DunedinPACE was somewhat more strongly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Levine PhenoAge clock (r = 0.36).
source: DunedinPACE was weakly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Horvath clock (r = 0.13) and somewhat more strongly correlated with age acceleration computed from the Hannum and Levine clocks (Hannum r = 0.26; PhenoAge r = 0.36).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data (n=1175).

claim: For the GrimAge clock, the correlation with the age-acceleration residuals was stronger (r = 0.58).
source: For the GrimAge clock proposed by Lu et al., the correlation with the age-acceleration residuals was stronger (r = 0.58).
evidence: Correlation was calculated from Understanding Society Study data (n=1175).

claim: Participants with faster DunedinPACE showed more advanced KDM Biological Age (r = 0.30 [0.24–0.36]).
source: Consistent with analysis of epigenetic age acceleration, participants with more advanced biological aging measured from physiological data also showed faster DunedinPACE (KDM Biological Age Advancement r = 0.30; Phenotypic Age Advancement r = 0.32; Homeostatic Dysregulation r = 0.09; Figure 3C).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data using physiology-based biological age measures.

claim: Participants with faster DunedinPACE showed more advanced Phenotypic Age (r = 0.32).
source: Consistent with analysis of epigenetic age acceleration, participants with more advanced biological aging measured from physiological data also showed faster DunedinPACE (KDM Biological Age Advancement r = 0.30; Phenotypic Age Advancement r = 0.32; Homeostatic Dysregulation r = 0.09; Figure 3C).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data using physiology-based biological age measures.

claim: Participants with faster DunedinPACE showed higher Homeostatic Dysregulation (r = 0.09).
source: Consistent with analysis of epigenetic age acceleration, participants with more advanced biological aging measured from physiological data also showed faster DunedinPACE (KDM Biological Age Advancement r = 0.30; Phenotypic Age Advancement r = 0.32; Homeostatic Dysregulation r = 0.09; Figure 3C).
evidence: Correlations were calculated from Understanding Society Study data using physiology-based biological age measures.

claim: The difference in DunedinPACE between those rating their health as excellent and poor was large (Cohen's d = 0.74 [0.46–1.03]).
source: The difference in DunedinPACE between those rating their health as excellent and poor was large (Cohen's d = 0.74 [0.46–1.03]; Figure 3C).
evidence: Effect size was calculated from Understanding Society Study data comparing self-rated health categories.

claim: In the NAS, participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for incident chronic disease morbidity (HR = 1.23 [1.07–1.42]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for morbidity and mortality (for incident chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE HR = 1.23 [1.07–1.42]; for prevalent chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE RR = 1.16 [1.12–1.20]; for mortality, DunedinPACE HR = 1.26 95% CI [1.14–1.40], Figure 4A).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from NAS data (n=771 older men, average age 77 years).

claim: In the NAS, participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for prevalent chronic disease morbidity (RR = 1.16 [1.12–1.20]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for morbidity and mortality (for incident chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE HR = 1.23 [1.07–1.42]; for prevalent chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE RR = 1.16 [1.12–1.20]; for mortality, DunedinPACE HR = 1.26 95% CI [1.14–1.40], Figure 4A).
evidence: Relative risks were calculated from NAS data (n=771 older men, average age 77 years).

claim: In the NAS, participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for mortality (HR = 1.26 95% CI [1.14–1.40]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE were at increased risk for morbidity and mortality (for incident chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE HR = 1.23 [1.07–1.42]; for prevalent chronic disease morbidity, DunedinPACE RR = 1.16 [1.12–1.20]; for mortality, DunedinPACE HR = 1.26 95% CI [1.14–1.40], Figure 4A).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from NAS data with follow-up from 1999-2013, during which 46% died.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for CVD (HR = 1.39 [1.26–1.54]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for CVD, stroke/TIA, and mortality (CVD HR = 1.39 [1.26–1.54]; stroke/TIA HR = 1.37 [1.19–1.58]; mortality HR = 1.65 95% CI [1.51–1.79], Figure 4B).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham Offspring cohort data (n=2471, 54% women, average age 66 years).

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for stroke/TIA (HR = 1.37 [1.19–1.58]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for CVD, stroke/TIA, and mortality (CVD HR = 1.39 [1.26–1.54]; stroke/TIA HR = 1.37 [1.19–1.58]; mortality HR = 1.65 95% CI [1.51–1.79], Figure 4B).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham Offspring cohort data with follow-up through 2018.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for mortality (HR = 1.65 95% CI [1.51–1.79]).
source: Participants with faster DunedinPACE at baseline were at increased risk for CVD, stroke/TIA, and mortality (CVD HR = 1.39 [1.26–1.54]; stroke/TIA HR = 1.37 [1.19–1.58]; mortality HR = 1.65 95% CI [1.51–1.79], Figure 4B).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham Offspring cohort data; 23% died over follow-up through 2018.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, participants with faster DunedinPACE were more likely to develop Nagi ADL disability (IRR = 1.40 [1.19–1.65]).
source: They were also more likely to develop disability (Nagi ADL IRR = 1.40 [1.19–1.65]; Katz ADL IRR = 1.33 [1.16–1.53]; Rosow-Breslau ADL IRR = 1.39 [1.24–1.56]).
evidence: Incidence rate ratios were calculated from Framingham Offspring cohort disability data through 2015.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study, participants with faster DunedinPACE were more likely to develop Katz ADL disability (IRR = 1.33 [1.16–1.53]).
source: They were also more likely to develop disability (Nagi ADL IRR = 1.40 [1.19–1.65]; Katz ADL IRR = 1.33 [1.16–1.53]; Rosow-Breslau ADL IRR = 1.39 [1.24–1.56]).

claim: E-Risk participants with low childhood socioeconomic status showed faster DunedinPACE compared to those with high childhood socioeconomic status (d = 0.38 95% CI [0.25–0.51]).
source: E-Risk participants with exposure to childhood poverty and victimization showed faster DunedinPACE (For low as compared to high childhood socioeconomic status, d = 0.38 95% CI [0.25–0.51]; for polyvictimization as compared to no victimization, d = 0.47 [0.17–0.77]; Figure 5).
evidence: Effect sizes were calculated from E-Risk Study data (n=1,658 members of 1994-1995 birth cohort, DNA methylation at age 18).

claim: E-Risk participants with polyvictimization showed faster DunedinPACE compared to those with no victimization (d = 0.47 [0.17–0.77]).
source: E-Risk participants with exposure to childhood poverty and victimization showed faster DunedinPACE (For low as compared to high childhood socioeconomic status, d = 0.38 95% CI [0.25–0.51]; for polyvictimization as compared to no victimization, d = 0.47 [0.17–0.77]; Figure 5).
evidence: Effect sizes were calculated from E-Risk Study data analyzing childhood victimization exposure (domestic violence, bullying, physical/sexual harm, neglect).

claim: In Framingham Heart Study analysis adjusted for GrimAge, DunedinPACE associations with mortality remained statistically different from zero (HR = 1.24 [1.49–1.74]).
source: In models adjusted for GrimAge, DunedinPACE associations with mortality, CVD, and disability were attenuated, but remained statistically different from zero (mortality HR = 1.24 [1.49–1.74], CVD HR = 1.18 [1.05–1.34], Nagi ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.02–1.58], Katz ADL IRR = 1.26 [1.02–1.54], Rosow-Breslau ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.08–1.50]); associations with stroke were similar to unadjusted models (HR = 1.33 [1.05–1.69]).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham data with covariate adjustment for GrimAge clock.

claim: In Framingham Heart Study analysis adjusted for GrimAge, DunedinPACE associations with CVD remained statistically different from zero (HR = 1.18 [1.05–1.34]).
source: In models adjusted for GrimAge, DunedinPACE associations with mortality, CVD, and disability were attenuated, but remained statistically different from zero (mortality HR = 1.24 [1.49–1.74], CVD HR = 1.18 [1.05–1.34], Nagi ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.02–1.58], Katz ADL IRR = 1.26 [1.02–1.54], Rosow-Breslau ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.08–1.50]); associations with stroke were similar to unadjusted models (HR = 1.33 [1.05–1.69]).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham data with covariate adjustment for GrimAge clock.

evidence: Incidence rate ratios were calculated from Framingham data with covariate adjustment for GrimAge clock.

source: In models adjusted for GrimAge, DunedinPACE associations with mortality, CVD, and disability were attenuated, but remained statistically different from zero (mortality HR = 1.24 [1.49–1.74], CVD HR = 1.18 [1.05–1.34], Nagi ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.02–1.58], Katz ADL IRR = 1.26 [1.02–1.54], Rosow-Breslau ADL IRR = 1.27 [1.08–1.50]); associations with stroke were similar to unadjusted models (HR = 1.33 [1.05–1.69]).
evidence: Hazard ratios were calculated from Framingham data with covariate adjustment for GrimAge clock.

claim: The Dunedin Study member with the slowest Pace of Aging aged by just 0.40 biological years per chronological year.
source: Over the two decades that we measured biological aging, the Study member with the slowest Pace of Aging aged by just 0.40 biological years per chronological year, while the Study member with the fastest Pace of Aging accrued 2.44 biological years per chronological year (Elliott et al., 2021b).
evidence: This value represents the extreme of the distribution from longitudinal Pace of Aging analysis in the Dunedin Study, as reported in Elliott et al., 2021b.

claim: The Dunedin Study member with the fastest Pace of Aging accrued 2.44 biological years per chronological year.
source: Over the two decades that we measured biological aging, the Study member with the slowest Pace of Aging aged by just 0.40 biological years per chronological year, while the Study member with the fastest Pace of Aging accrued 2.44 biological years per chronological year (Elliott et al., 2021b).
evidence: This value represents the extreme of the distribution from longitudinal Pace of Aging analysis in the Dunedin Study, as reported in Elliott et al., 2021b.

claim: Study members showed wide variation in their Pace of Aging (Mean = 1 biological year per chronological year, SD = 0.29).
source: Study members showed wide variation in their Pace of Aging (Mean = 1 biological year per chronological year, SD = 0.29).
evidence: Descriptive statistics from the Dunedin Study Pace of Aging analysis.

claim: The final DunedinPACE algorithm included 173 CpG sites.
source: The resulting algorithm included 173 CpG sites.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of the DunedinPACE algorithm derived from elastic-net regression.

claim: Elastic-net regression analysis to develop DunedinPACE included the subset of probes with acceptable test-retest reliability (ICC >0.4, n = 81,2392).
source: Analysis included the subset of probes included on both the Illumina 450 k and EPIC arrays which we previously determined to have acceptable test-retest reliability (ICC >0.4, n = 81,2392) (Sugden et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the probe selection criteria for the machine learning analysis, based on prior reliability analysis by Sugden et al., 2020.

claim: The alpha parameter of the elastic net was fixed at 0.5.
source: Following the method established by Horvath, 2013 and used in our prior analysis, we fixed the alpha parameter of the elastic net at 0.5.
evidence: This is a methodological choice following established practice from Horvath, 2013.

claim: The final lambda value selected by the elastic net analysis was 0.042.
source: The final lamda value selected by the analysis was 0.042.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the parameter value from the elastic-net regression analysis.

claim: Participant-reported smoking history explained 30% of variance in DunedinPoAm in the Understanding Society Study.
source: In follow-up analysis of the Understanding Society Study, we found that participant-reported smoking history explained 30% of variance in DunedinPoAm, but only 13% of variance in DunedinPACE.
evidence: R-squared values from regression analysis in Understanding Society Study data.

claim: Participant-reported smoking history explained 13% of variance in DunedinPACE in the Understanding Society Study.
source: In follow-up analysis of the Understanding Society Study, we found that participant-reported smoking history explained 30% of variance in DunedinPoAm, but only 13% of variance in DunedinPACE.
evidence: R-squared values from regression analysis in Understanding Society Study data.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study Offspring Cohort, smoking history explained 23% of variance in DunedinPoAm.
source: Results were similar in analysis of the Framingham Heart Study Offspring Cohort (R2 = 23% for DunedinPoAm vs. 12% for DunedinPACE).
evidence: R-squared values from regression analysis in Framingham data.

claim: In the Framingham Heart Study Offspring Cohort, smoking history explained 12% of variance in DunedinPACE.
source: Results were similar in analysis of the Framingham Heart Study Offspring Cohort (R2 = 23% for DunedinPoAm vs. 12% for DunedinPACE).
evidence: R-squared values from regression analysis in Framingham data.

claim: Model-organism studies are yielding treatments that slow the accumulation of deterioration in cells and organs.
source: Guided by research on the cellular hallmarks of aging, model-organism studies are yielding treatments that slow the accumulation of deterioration in cells and organs (Barzilai et al., 2018; Bellantuono, 2018; Campisi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research on model-organism studies.

claim: Human geroprotector trials face a barrier when it comes to outcome measures because humans' long lifespan makes it prohibitively time-consuming to test whether a treatment extends healthspan.
source: However, human geroprotector trials face a barrier when it comes to outcome measures: humans' long lifespan makes it prohibitively time-consuming to test whether a treatment extends healthspan (Justice et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Justice et al., 2018 discussing challenges in human trials.

claim: The process of biological aging is ongoing in healthy young adults.
source: We originally applied this design to test the geroscience-derived hypothesis that the process of biological aging was ongoing in healthy young adults and, critically, that it was already variable across individuals decades before most chronic diseases onset (Belsky et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2021b).
evidence: This hypothesis was tested in the Dunedin Study and is supported by citations to prior publications.

claim: Biological aging is already variable across individuals decades before most chronic diseases onset.
source: We originally applied this design to test the geroscience-derived hypothesis that the process of biological aging was ongoing in healthy young adults and, critically, that it was already variable across individuals decades before most chronic diseases onset (Belsky et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2021b).
evidence: This hypothesis was tested in the Dunedin Study and is supported by citations to prior publications.

claim: Aging can be understood as gradual, progressive deterioration simultaneously affecting different organ systems.
source: Because aging can be understood as gradual, progressive deterioration simultaneously affecting different organ systems, we tracked declines in the cardiovascular, metabolic, renal, hepatic, immune, periodontal, and pulmonary systems of each participant using multiple biomarker measurements of each organ system, first at ages 26, 32, and 38 years, and subsequently including a fourth assessment at age 45 years.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about aging that underlies the study design and is consistent with geroscience theory.

claim: People with faster Pace of Aging tend to experience more rapid aging-related decline in physical and cognitive functions.
source: People with faster Pace of Aging tend to experience more rapid aging-related decline in physical and cognitive functions and develop early signs of brain aging (Belsky et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2021a; Elliott et al., 2021b; Rasmussen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on the Dunedin Study Pace of Aging measure.

claim: People with faster Pace of Aging develop early signs of brain aging.
source: People with faster Pace of Aging tend to experience more rapid aging-related decline in physical and cognitive functions and develop early signs of brain aging (Belsky et al., 2015; Elliott et al., 2021a; Elliott et al., 2021b; Rasmussen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on the Dunedin Study Pace of Aging measure.

claim: Intervention to slow Pace of Aging could preserve functions lost with aging and extend healthspan.
source: This evidence suggests that intervention to slow Pace of Aging could preserve functions lost with aging and extend healthspan.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the evidence that faster Pace of Aging is associated with functional decline.

claim: People with faster DunedinPoAm scores more often experienced declines in cognitive and physical functioning by midlife.
source: Like the original Pace of Aging, people with faster DunedinPoAm scores more often experienced declines in cognitive and physical functioning by midlife and showed more rapid facial aging Belsky et al., 2020; in older adults, faster DunedinPoAm predicted increased risk of disease and death (Belsky et al., 2020; Graf et al., 2021); in young people, experiences of early-life adversity were linked to faster DunedinPoAm (Belsky et al., 2020; Raffington et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on DunedinPoAm.

claim: People with faster DunedinPoAm showed more rapid facial aging.
source: Like the original Pace of Aging, people with faster DunedinPoAm scores more often experienced declines in cognitive and physical functioning by midlife and showed more rapid facial aging Belsky et al., 2020; in older adults, faster DunedinPoAm predicted increased risk of disease and death (Belsky et al., 2020; Graf et al., 2021); in young people, experiences of early-life adversity were linked to faster DunedinPoAm (Belsky et al., 2020; Raffington et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Belsky et al., 2020.

claim: In older adults, faster DunedinPoAm predicted increased risk of disease and death.
source: Like the original Pace of Aging, people with faster DunedinPoAm scores more often experienced declines in cognitive and physical functioning by midlife and showed more rapid facial aging Belsky et al., 2020; in older adults, faster DunedinPoAm predicted increased risk of disease and death (Belsky et al., 2020; Graf et al., 2021); in young people, experiences of early-life adversity were linked to faster DunedinPoAm (Belsky et al., 2020; Raffington et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Belsky et al., 2020 and Graf et al., 2021.

claim: In young people, experiences of early-life adversity were linked to faster DunedinPoAm.
source: Like the original Pace of Aging, people with faster DunedinPoAm scores more often experienced declines in cognitive and physical functioning by midlife and showed more rapid facial aging Belsky et al., 2020; in older adults, faster DunedinPoAm predicted increased risk of disease and death (Belsky et al., 2020; Graf et al., 2021); in young people, experiences of early-life adversity were linked to faster DunedinPoAm (Belsky et al., 2020; Raffington et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Belsky et al., 2020 and Raffington et al., 2021.

claim: DunedinPoAm had only moderate test-retest reliability.
source: In addition, similar to other DNA methylation composites measured from microarray data, the measure had only moderate test-retest reliability (Higgins-Chen et al., 2021), limiting its value to clinical trials seeking to test within-participant changes from pre-treatment baseline to post-treatment follow-up.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Higgins-Chen et al., 2021.

claim: DunedinPACE is distinct from the DNA methylation clocks in the method of its design and in its interpretation.
source: As a new DNA methylation measure of biological aging, DunedinPACE joins a well-established battery of DNA methylation measures known as 'clocks', so-named for their accurate prediction of chronological age (Horvath and Raj, 2018). However, DunedinPACE is distinct from the DNA methylation clocks in the method of its design and in its interpretation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the conceptual and methodological distinction between DunedinPACE and DNA methylation clocks.

claim: DunedinPACE is derived from analysis of longitudinal data collected from a cohort of individuals who are all the same chronological age.
source: DunedinPACE is derived from analysis of longitudinal data collected from a cohort of individuals who are all the same chronological age.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design used to develop DunedinPACE.

claim: DunedinPACE reflects differences between individuals in the rate of deterioration in system integrity occurring over a fixed time interval, age 26 to age 45 years.
source: It reflects differences between those individuals in the rate of deterioration in system integrity occurring over a fixed time interval, age 26 to age 45 years.
evidence: This is a direct statement about what DunedinPACE measures.

claim: Analysis of a single-year birth cohort distinguishes aging from confounding effects of exposures to factors that alter the methylome and that differ across generations (cohort effects).
source: It therefore has three distinguishing features that isolate aging from other confounds: (1) analysis of a single-year birth cohort distinguishes aging from confounding effects of exposures to factors that alter the methylome and that differ across generations, referred to hereafter as 'cohort effects'; (2) initiation of follow-up in young adults distinguishes aging from the effects of disease and excludes contamination from survival bias; and (3) focus on changes in multi-organ-system integrity during adult life distinguishes ongoing aging processes from deficits established early in development.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about how the study design controls for confounding.

claim: Initiation of follow-up in young adults distinguishes aging from the effects of disease and excludes contamination from survival bias.
source: It therefore has three distinguishing features that isolate aging from other confounds: (1) analysis of a single-year birth cohort distinguishes aging from confounding effects of exposures to factors that alter the methylome and that differ across generations, referred to hereafter as 'cohort effects'; (2) initiation of follow-up in young adults distinguishes aging from the effects of disease and excludes contamination from survival bias; and (3) focus on changes in multi-organ-system integrity during adult life distinguishes ongoing aging processes from deficits established early in development.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about how the study design controls for confounding.

claim: Focus on changes in multi-organ-system integrity during adult life distinguishes ongoing aging processes from deficits established early in development.
source: It therefore has three distinguishing features that isolate aging from other confounds: (1) analysis of a single-year birth cohort distinguishes aging from confounding effects of exposures to factors that alter the methylome and that differ across generations, referred to hereafter as 'cohort effects'; (2) initiation of follow-up in young adults distinguishes aging from the effects of disease and excludes contamination from survival bias; and (3) focus on changes in multi-organ-system integrity during adult life distinguishes ongoing aging processes from deficits established early in development.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about how the study design controls for confounding.

claim: The DNA methylation clocks were developed using a single cross-section of data from samples of mixed-age and older adults.
source: The clocks, in contrast, were developed using a single cross-section of data from samples of mixed-age and older adults.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used to develop DNA methylation clocks, based on established knowledge of how these measures were created.

claim: The DNA methylation clocks do not distinguish aging from cohort effects.
source: They do not distinguish aging from cohort effects, are vulnerable to survival bias and contamination of aging signal by disease processes, and do not distinguish aging-related changes from prenatal/childhood deficits.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of DNA methylation clocks based on their cross-sectional, mixed-age design.

claim: The DNA methylation clocks are vulnerable to survival bias and contamination of aging signal by disease processes.
source: They do not distinguish aging from cohort effects, are vulnerable to survival bias and contamination of aging signal by disease processes, and do not distinguish aging-related changes from prenatal/childhood deficits.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of DNA methylation clocks based on their cross-sectional design in older adults.

claim: The DNA methylation clocks do not distinguish aging-related changes from prenatal/childhood deficits.
source: They do not distinguish aging from cohort effects, are vulnerable to survival bias and contamination of aging signal by disease processes, and do not distinguish aging-related changes from prenatal/childhood deficits.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of DNA methylation clocks based on their methodology.

claim: The Dunedin Study is a 1972-1973 birth cohort (N = 1037).
source: We developed the DunedinPACE measure reported here by analyzing the pace of biological aging in a 1972–1973 birth cohort (N = 1037), the Dunedin Study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: The longer follow-up period and additional measurement occasion improve the power and precision of modeling longitudinal change in system integrity.
source: The longer follow-up period, which allowed us to observe more aging-related change in system integrity, and the additional measurement occasion included in analysis improve the power and precision of our modeling of longitudinal change in system integrity (Brandmaier et al., 2018; Rast and Hofer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological literature on longitudinal modeling.

claim: The refined DNA-methylation dataset used for machine-learning improves reliability of measurement.

evidence: This is an inference based on the restriction of analysis to probes with higher test-retest reliability.

claim: Both four-time-points to measure Pace of Aging and restricting machine-learning analysis to CpG sites with higher test-retest reliability contributed to the technical improvement in DunedinPACE over DunedinPoAm.
source: Results suggest that both four-time-points to measure Pace of Aging and restricting machine-learning analysis to CpG sites with higher test-retest reliability contributed to the technical improvement in DunedinPACE over DunedinPoAm (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis reported in Appendix 1.

claim: In humans and many other species, the increase in mortality risk with advancing chronological age is nonlinear, suggesting that the pace of biological aging accelerates as we grow older.
source: In humans and many other species, the increase in mortality risk with advancing chronological age is nonlinear, suggesting that the pace of biological aging accelerates as we grow older (Gompertz, 1997; Kirkwood, 2015; Olshansky and Carnes, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to demographic and aging literature.

claim: DunedinPACE is as reliable as the GrimAge clock.
source: DunedinPACE is as reliable as the GrimAge clock and more reliable in comparison to the other clocks, although methods have been proposed that may improve reliabilities for the other clocks (Higgins-Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on ICC values shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: DunedinPACE is more reliable in comparison to the Horvath, Hannum, and PhenoAge clocks.
source: DunedinPACE is as reliable as the GrimAge clock and more reliable in comparison to the other clocks, although methods have been proposed that may improve reliabilities for the other clocks (Higgins-Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on ICC values shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Higgins-Chen et al., 2021.

claim: DunedinPACE associations with health-span endpoints were little-changed by covariate adjustment for the Horvath, Hannum, or PhenoAge Clocks.
source: DunedinPACE associations with health-span endpoints were little-changed by covariate adjustment for the Horvath, Hannum, or PhenoAge Clocks.
evidence: This is based on analysis in the Framingham Heart Study testing incremental predictive validity.

claim: DunedinPACE adds incremental prediction over and above all clocks studied.
source: Thus, Dunedin PACE adds incremental prediction over and above all clocks studied here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis showing DunedinPACE associations remained significant after adjusting for other clocks.
